lesson.title: The Weight of Air: Measuring Atmospheric Pressure
lesson.summary: Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the column of air above you, and it is measured with a barometer and expressed in units such as atmospheres, millimeters of mercury, or kilopascals.
lesson.body:
Gas pressure, as you learned previously, comes from countless particle collisions against a surface. The air around you is a gas, so it too exerts pressure, simply because it is made of trillions of nitrogen and oxygen molecules constantly colliding with everything they touch, including your skin, the ground, and the surface of any liquid. Atmospheric pressure specifically refers to the pressure exerted by the entire column of air sitting above a given point on Earth's surface. The higher up you go, the less air is above you pressing down, which is why atmospheric pressure drops steadily as altitude increases and why it becomes noticeably harder to breathe on a tall mountain: fewer air molecules occupy the same volume, so fewer collisions occur with each breath.

Atmospheric pressure is measured with a barometer, a sealed tube of mercury inverted in a mercury reservoir. The air pressure pushing down on the reservoir supports a column of mercury inside the tube, and the height of that column tells you the pressure. At sea level, under standard conditions, this column reaches 760 millimeters, which defines standard atmospheric pressure. Because this measurement technique is so historically important, several equivalent units of pressure are all still in everyday use: 1 atmosphere (atm) equals 760 millimeters of mercury (mmHg), which equals 760 torr, which equals 101.325 kilopascals (kPa), which equals about 14.7 pounds per square inch (psi). All four describe exactly the same physical pressure; they are just different rulers for measuring it.

Converting between these units is mostly a matter of setting up a ratio from the equivalencies above. Suppose a weather station reports a barometric reading of 745 mmHg. To express this in atmospheres, divide by the number of mmHg in one atm: 745 mmHg times (1 atm / 760 mmHg) = 0.980 atm. To express it in kilopascals, multiply by the kPa-per-atm conversion instead: 745 mmHg times (101.325 kPa / 760 mmHg) = 75,487.125 / 760 = 99.3 kPa. Both answers describe the same day's weather; a reading of 745 mmHg is slightly below the standard 760 mmHg, which is typical of a low-pressure weather system.

Keep this 745 mmHg reading in mind. It will come back later in this unit when we calculate the pressure of a gas collected over water, because in that kind of experiment the total pressure you measure with a barometer, minus the pressure contributed by water vapor, tells you the pressure of the gas you actually care about. That calculation depends on Dalton's law of partial pressures, which is covered a few chapters ahead, but the raw atmospheric pressure reading you just learned to convert is exactly the kind of number that calculation starts from.
